sections.title: Thinking vs feeling you can change
2. Are you interested in the next steps?

blocks.p: The self-narrative is what paradigm-building has been leading up to. You understand the Polyvagal Theory on a cognitive level: the biology, trauma, and the importance of connection. Knowing is not good enough, though. A nostalgic phrase from my childhood speaks volumes here: "Knowing is half the battle" (G.I. Joe). It's not sufficient to simply know; you must also apply that knowledge. When you apply the Polyvagal paradigm to your own life, it helps build your narrative.

A self-narrative is a story you have around yourself: who you are, how you are, why you are, your worth in life: to yourself and others, your potential in life, your responsibility to make a change, the role of your parents then and now, why events in your life did or did not unfold how you needed them to, and how lovable you are or are not. The answers to these things are all narratives, for better or worse.
So, let's take things to the next step and start crafting a new narrative.

Every single one of us has an autonomic nervous system (ANS). The function of our ANS is to increase our chances of survival. Even though we don't live in the wild, surviving from moment to moment, these biological functions still exist within us and affect our daily lives. Humans have largely conquered the external natural world but not the internal. We still, and forever will be, organisms driven by our internal state.

Our Polyvagal state determines everything about us, from the past, present, and future. The state of our bodies dictates every moment: sensations, impulses, emotions, cognitions, and behaviors. Your interactions with others, motivation for success, and capacity to welcome love... it's all limited or expanded by your state.

You have these Polyvagal states within you, just like anyone else. These social or defensive states activate or deactivate throughout your existence in the tiniest moments and throughout the entirety of your life, from birth to death. You are inescapably a mammal needing to survive, no matter the luxuries or stresses of life. In this way, we're the same.

I know you have a different life than I do, and I've had a different life than the next person. I know. But all three of us, and the rest of humanity, have an autonomic nervous system. We each use neuroception. We each need co-regulation. We each need a stronger vagal brake. And on and on. We're mammals. We're organisms. Our bodies must survive and exist in different states to ensure that happens.

But we probably have no idea what's happening within us and the potential of our state. How could we? We're not taught this stuff as kids: not in school, heck, probably not even in graduate-level psychology school. If anything, we go to great lengths to avoid or numb our defensive states. We focus on the words in our brains. We've treated our natural impulses as alien invaders and need to rid ourselves of them.

Sadly, we're probably more disconnected from the internal world than ever. Our states shift without our conscious awareness. Our impulses to self-regulate go unnoticed. We focus on the myriad screens in front of us and whatever they bark incessantly every moment.

At least, I hope that's how things used to be for you, from now on. I hope this helps you gain more clarity or curiosity about your internal world. I hope you realize there's more going on internally than you once knew, and I hope you're now more open to it. There's still a long way to go, but you've taken strong first steps.
I hope that you are thinking differently about yourself. I hope the Polyvagal Theory knowledge lays a new foundation to build on. At a minimum, reflect on these basic core ideas:

ul: Your body can be in a state of more or less safety or defense.
Your body's state is not a choice you make; it's a reaction to safety or danger cues.
Your body may have gotten stuck in a state of defense due to past contexts.
Trauma is not necessarily permanent; you can access more safety and reduce defensive activation.
As you get unstuck from defense, you will experience more connection and emotional freedom.

blocks.p: All of these core ideas apply to you as much as anyone else. You are no different than the next. Your experiences are your own and won't exactly match another's. But you're still human. You're still a mammal, just like they are. The way your body responds to events is a natural result of this, just like the next person.
You're not broken, defective, or abnormal. It's possible to get stuck in defense as a natural and normal result of your life's context.

blocks.prompt: Do you have an autonomic nervous system? (yes or no)
Does your ANS shift your Polyvagal state? (yes or no)
Do you have conscious control over your state? (yes or no)
Did you have conscious control over your state in the past? Or did your state shift based on what it needed? (yes or no)
Are you currently stuck in a state of defense? (yes, no, or sometimes)
Is it normal for someone to get stuck in a defensive state? (yes or no)

blocks.p: If we take all this information so far and boil it down to its bare bones, this is what we're left with: stuck not broken. Your trauma is an issue of being stuck in an autonomic state of defense. It's an issue of having less access to and development of safety pathways to allow and release the stuck defensive energy. It's an issue of neurocepting danger and not safety. It's an issue of stories in our thoughts that are not helpful. And behaviors that keep us in defensive feedback loops rather than self-regulate.

Your frustrations with yourself are not an issue of being broken. Or of being wrong. Or of being defective. This is about being stuck. Stuck as a biological organism. Your Autonomic Nervous System might be in a stuck state of defense. But there's some really good news here.
Stuckness is not defeat; it's possibility. There's hope in stuckness.

If you're stuck, this means you can get unstuck. It means you can calm the self-defeating thoughts that cloud your mind. You can change your behaviors. You can live with more emotional freedom. Stuck means your brainstem can still neurocept safety and climb the Polyvagal ladder.

Being stuck also means you can move forward on your hopes and dreams in life. You don't need to get unstuck all at once and likely won't. The goal is of course to get as unstuck as possible, but that's in the future and we don't know when that will happen. But in the present moment, you can take a step toward unstuckness.

You've already taken steps forward. You've begun by laying the foundation of a new paradigm and narrative. And I'd bet you've also done other things to take steps forward, like going to therapy, silent retreats, yoga, meditation, online groups, paid courses, guided substance use, and potentially a plethora of other things.

Based on what we have covered, Stuck Not Broken is one potential new narrative for yourself. Another could be that your body did what it needed to do to survive. Whether that was during your upbringing or a specific life event, your body did what it needed to. It's to be celebrated, admired and thanked.

I know I'm talking as if the body is separate from you. I mean it in this sense, your autonomic nervous system, acting underneath your conscious direction and even outside your conscious choice, made shifts to survive. Your body, through the brainstem and ANS, did what it needed to. It does all the time, even now. These shifts are constantly happening within you in big and small ways. But your upbringing or that specific moment required action from your ANS, and it did its job. It got you through that moment. It got you through your childhood intact enough to be where you are now.

None of this means life is great, or good in the least. Maybe your life is downright s***. Maybe. Nevertheless, while that may be true, it's also true that you're here. You're aware enough to learn new information and form a new understanding of yourself. Things could be worse. I swear this is not a dismissal; it's simply a fact. You can honor your history while also appreciating the present, your efforts, and the possibilities of the future.

Stuckness is not a bad thing: it's a normal thing based on the context of our lives. It might feel like a "bad" thing, but it's not in its essence. In fact, we're each stuck in some way: even the person who seems to have everything together and is accomplishing everything they want. They've got the house, the family, and the money. But this doesn't mean they have self-regulation. It doesn't mean they have access to their safety state. A stuck defensive state could have driven all those things they've accumulated and milestones they've checked off.

The person in their stuck fight state could use that to their advantage. They could use that to overpower their colleagues and aggressively get promotions, no matter who they have to trample. That energy could fuel a "hustle" entrepreneurial mindset. But that doesn't equate to happiness. Anyone can be stuck; it just looks different from person to person.

How many people don't find the opportunity to learn, self-reflect, and create a new narrative? Before hearing about the Polyvagal Theory, you may not have found the opportunity. You may not have had it a week ago or two months ago. But now you do. Now you can see your stuckness more clearly. Maybe you can see what obstacles are in your way, whether cognitive, behavioral, environmental, familial, social, or something else.

You'll be better prepared to consider life when you are less stuck and more free. You'll work on new ways of feeling, thinking, and behaving by practicing the internal work and eventually actively allowing the shifts to take place. This practice will lay a solid foundation for regulation, no matter what life throws at you or what you want to take on.

You've found your current stuck point, and that's great. It's the one that brought you here. And I sincerely hope you get unstuck from this current stuck point. But there will be another one. In fact, I hope there is another. For both of us, the next stuck point is simply an opportunity to grow further. It's an opportunity to expand our potential for emotional freedom, deeper connections, and more accomplishments. Personal growth is all about finding stuck points and meeting them through self-regulation.

However, the next stuck point may be due to something other than dysregulation from past events. It might be because there is dysregulation from current or future events. As in, there is something new you are accomplishing, and you don't have the vagal brake required for this new thing. Yet. Like starting a business, reconnecting with old friends, or working on a relationship. These are things that you want to accomplish now and in the future. You'll have the regulation necessary to address these; it might feel awkward. Anxiety-producing. Different. Vulnerable. Exposed. But that's okay. It's not about the old stuff. At least, not as much. It's just new and different and requires a new level of safety anchoring.
I hope the Stuck Not Broken narrative is useful for you. I hope you can apply this to yourself and soften defensive state activation. I hope it adds a warm, normalizing layer to your self-narratives.

blocks.prompt: Take a moment and remind yourself that you're laying the foundations of change. You're working on top-down understandings, potentially updating your beliefs about yourself and others.
Is there room in your self-concept to shift from seeing "stuck" as an obstacle into an opportunity?
What could you accomplish when you get a little less stuck? How about a lot less? What would life be like?
What can you appreciate about your life right now?

blocks.p: What I've laid out might make sense, and that's great. But I want to remind you that your efforts to change are all about you. The larger knowledge is important (paradigm). Applying it to yourself is also important (narrative). One of the obstacles to applying it to yourself could be your belief or lack of belief in making your own change.

I want you to answer that question honestly. Is change generally possible? Can someone change their life? Can they change their Polyvagal state? Can they anchor in safety and feel more calm, confident, and connected? I'll assume we agree change is generally possible. Next question.
Is change possible for you? Answer that honestly.

You may think your life cannot improve, even though you know it's generally possible for others. You may think your Polyvagal state cannot improve. You may think you're permanently stuck in your current state and circumstances. That's a problem. That's an obstacle to growth. Believing you can't change comes from your Polyvagal state ("story follows state"). Ideally, you change your state, and then your belief changes. But first, I want to convince you that you're wrong.

I want to challenge your thinking, nudge you toward more curiosity about your potential to change, and deconstruct your self-defeating thoughts about your change potential. Deconstructing your thoughts doesn't solve the problem, I know, but it helps open up an opportunity for a thought replacement or reframe. Introducing a new thought can act as a top-down state shifter.

You've learned the Polyvagal Theory, but now we need that knowledge to penetrate further. The knowledge is nearly useless if you don't believe you can make change. I want to take the general knowledge that change is possible for others and apply it directly to you. I am going to discuss this from a few different angles. I'll give you more prompts to journal or reflect on. Just be honest with yourself as you do so.

blocks.prompt: Do you believe you can make change?

blocks.p: People change. You've seen it directly or heard of others changing their lives for the better. There was an autobiography that you read about some celebrity changing. You've seen someone on TikTok talking about the changes they've made. You've watched a documentary on an athlete who made change. Or someone talking about their changes in a Ted Talk. Someone you know has improved their own life: a friend, a relative, or your kids. The point is: people have changed. They can. And at some point in your life, you've seen it.

I'm not saying that because others have made positive changes, you should also be able to. Nor that you must. Not exactly. This Polyvagal state shift stuff isn't a switch we turn off and on. Others have made change, which is evidence that change is generally, factually, a possibility. What that looks like for you, how it feels, and how difficult it is, I don't really know. You'll have to discover that as you go.
Factually, change is possible. Factually, other people have done so.

You've probably gotten this far by trying self-care or trauma recovery techniques, which have shown some benefits. You've probably already seen some change within yourself or at least glimpses of what change might look like. Change is generally possible, and you've probably experienced some level of positive change within yourself.

blocks.prompt: Has anything been helpful in your trauma recovery or self-development journey so far?
What have you tried that was really helpful? What was a little helpful? What was not helpful at all?
Are you somehow different or incapable of change?
Who is one person you know who has made a significant positive change in their life? (Or someone you don't know personally.)

blocks.p: Again, factually, you've already made changes in the past. There's probably a time in your life when you made a positive change. There's probably a time when you accomplished something, even when you didn't think you would. You've probably tasted success before.

Think back to a time in your life when you felt successful, content, or accomplished. Those feelings come when you've completed something and gone from point A to point B. You went from an experience of wanting to an experience of fulfilling that want. Even in a micro example, you changed.

Think back to a time when you felt excited, motivated, or focused on a goal. If you've ever felt this way, you've had the capacity for change in the past. And that indicates you can have it again. I'll point out the obvious again: you're reading this. Not only have you felt motivated for change in the past, but you have it within you now, and you're acting on it.

blocks.h3: Thinking vs feeling you can change

blocks.p: I hope you're starting to shift your thinking about the possibilities to make a change in your life. I'm attempting to address the logical, factual possibilities of change. But even if you were to agree with me on the logical basis of possibly changing, that doesn't mean you would feel it.

Thinking something and feeling something are different. To feel we can change involves hope and motivation. Hope comes from activating the ventral vagal safety pathways. Motivation comes from flight/fight mobilization along with ventral vagal safety.

But, if you didn't have at least a little motivation and hope, you wouldn't have gotten this far. You already have at least a little motivation and hope within you. You already have at least some of the main ingredients for feeling you can change and not just thinking change is possible.
But maybe you don't feel or recognize it. So, let's take another angle. You may already have an emotion we can tap into and use for change. Ask yourself these two questions:

If you feel fed up, there's energy in your system. That tells me you have some mobility (flight/fight) activation. Since you have mobility, you simply need a bit more safety to turn that activation into motivation, focus, determination, and empowerment. Let the fed-up energy be there and continue on. The important thing to recognize for now is that you're already energized and investing your time into this. You're on the path of change already.

blocks.h3: 2. Are you interested in the next steps?

blocks.p: If you're interested in the next steps, that tells me you have some safety in your system: ventral vagal safety results in curiosity, interest, and eagerness to learn. Your safety pathways may be guiding you to the next step, felt as interest. Interest also tells me there's some mobility within you.
Reflect on those two questions if you think you can change but not feel it. The mobilization you're feeling is a feeling of change. It's a pull toward growth.

Yep. Once again, the fact that you're reading this is evidence of your change. If you're learning something new, that means you're changing: at least a little bit. It starts with knowledge, right? So, this is the first step in your change process.
No one makes a change all at once. They do many things: learn, unlearn, fail, experiment, try something else, and do it all again. This might be your first step. Regardless, change is occurring.
